title: After My Clerkship at Duke University
paragraphs: At the end of March 2006, I set out from Nagoya, still a little chilly with the cherry blossoms not yet in bloom, for Durham in North Carolina, in the northeastern United States. Wrapped in anticipation and anxiety about the three-month medical student clerkship and unable to sleep soundly, I arrived at a city that gave the impression of a relaxed country town. At last, the clerkship at Duke University Hospital that I had long awaited was beginning. Duke University was founded in 1924 and is relatively new among American universities, but it is known as a famous private university in the United States. It is a university hospital offering cutting-edge treatment and various services, and many patients came all the way from neighbouring states. Its medical school also has a somewhat unique curriculum different from other schools and enjoys tremendous popularity, and excellent students gather there. In such a blessed environment, I trained in ophthalmology, hematology and medical oncology. Below, I would like to tell you in turn the outline of the clerkship in each department and my impressions. In ophthalmology, I spent four weeks centred on outpatient clerkship and observing surgery. Rotating week by week through specialty clinics such as cornea, glaucoma and retina, I joined the team practice carried out by residents, fellows and attendings. For the first two weeks I simply watched, overwhelmed by the English flowing past at a dizzying speed and by the clinical practice. But in the third week, during my clerkship at the Veterans Hospital, I was given the chance to first examine patients on my own, present to the resident and attending, and then see the patients together with them. Struggling in front of the patient with a slit-lamp microscope and a lens, I had a thoroughly enjoyable clerkship. I realised that even if I did not understand much, if I showed motivation and made an effort, it would be appreciated. Lectures for residents were held several times a week, and the explanations by attendings who are actually familiar with both clinical practice and training were practical and interesting, and conveyed strongly how broad and fascinating the field of ophthalmology is. By chance, in the fourth week there was a workshop held every year by the Duke retina team, and it was an honour to be present at a place where experts gathered from around the world. In hematology, I spent three weeks mainly on the consult team. Twice a week I also attended the coagulation disorders clinic and the sickle cell clinic, and I was allowed to examine many patients. When there were many patients, team consultations by residents, fellows and attendings went on until nearly 8 p.m., and seeing them place test orders after that, my fantasy that American doctors work from nine to five was blown away completely. A hematology conference and a joint hematology-oncology conference were each held once a week early in the morning, with presentations by many doctors and lively discussion. Through these I could see the form that EBM takes in the United States: starting a discussion from reports in many papers, adding the empirical knowledge of many attendings to it in heated debate, and thereby approaching practice with the treatment suited to each patient. It also stays in my mind how the fellows trained the presentation and discussion abilities that are essential for specialists through these many opportunities to present. The last was medical oncology. On Mondays and Thursdays I joined the team practice on the oncology ward, and on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Fridays I attended the oncology clinic. They were busy days, and even in my third month it was a struggle to get used to each team, but supported by warm-hearted doctors and co-medical staff, I was able to make it a fruitful four weeks. Medical oncologists are specialists in chemotherapy, and since, apart from hematological diseases, almost all administration of anticancer drugs to tumours is done in the oncology clinic, the patients admitted to the oncology ward are mainly those whose condition has worsened and who need acute-phase treatment. Although both are grouped under the same name of medical oncology, practice in the clinic and practice on the ward are very different, and I was very fortunate to have the chance to see both, which stand in a relationship of light and shadow. Since the aim on the ward is acute-phase treatment, once a patient's condition stabilises, they either go home or move to a hospice. On several occasions I faced situations in which we had to urge a move to a hospice, and the atmosphere, more severe even than a cancer diagnosis, left me breathless. Although I could not get involved on the ward because each case was too serious, in the clinic I was allowed to examine various patients, such as new patients and those under follow-up, and I was blessed with the chance to see many cases. As befits a facility known as one of the foremost cancer treatment centres in the country, the patients were mainly those seeking second opinions or cutting-edge clinical trials, and I keenly felt each person's tenacity to survive. Teamwork functioned well so that such patients could be seen efficiently one after another, and I felt that an environment had been set up in which the doctors' abundant medical knowledge could be devoted solely to deciding treatment policy. There were many times when getting used to so many things was tiring, but for that very reason I fully enjoyed American culture too, taking short trips on days off, enjoying sports games and films with friends I made there, and attending home parties. By placing myself in medical care in the United States, which is often compared as the representative of a medical system different from Japan's, and having the chance to experience its advantages and disadvantages, I conversely came to feel how well developed Japanese medical care is. Of course, I cannot deny that there are things to learn from the United States, but gaining a perspective from which I can appreciate the good points of Japan was the greatest gain. I would like to express my deep gratitude to Dr. 小林, Dr. 伊藤, Dr. Fields, and 鈴木-san and 西尾-san of the administrative office and the many other people who gave me this irreplaceable opportunity and always supported me, and I hope that more students will actively take advantage of this system and receive diverse stimulation in the future.
